name: State of Franklin
label: Franklin
source: Declared at Jonesborough, 14 December 1784 (Statehood Campaigns outline, Appendix A; Tennessee Encyclopedia, "State of Franklin"); its counties: S. C. Williams, History of the Lost State of Franklin (1924), the three North Carolina counties of Washington, Sullivan and Greene
note: Drawn as those three counties on the day it was declared, from the Newberry's county lines. North Carolina never fixed Greene County's western limit (the Newberry), so the shape runs west to the Mississippi, round Davidson County (the Cumberland settlements): wider than the East Tennessee Franklin governed. Franklin's own counties of 1785 (Spencer, Caswell, Sevier, Wayne, Blount) had no legal lines and are not drawn. Over by early 1789: the end is known to the year, drawn dashed. Not yet reviewed by the owner.

name: Territory of Colorado (the Pico Act)
label: Territory of Colorado
counties: San Luis Obispo|Santa Barbara|Los Angeles|San Diego|San Bernardino
source: Statutes of California, 1859, chapter 288, approved 18 April 1859: "including the counties of San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara, Los Angeles, San Diego, San Bernardino, and a part of Buena Vista"; approved by the voters of those counties on 7 September 1859 (J. M. Guinn, 1905; Statehood Campaigns outline, Appendix A)
note: Drawn as the five counties the act names, on the day it was approved, from the Newberry's county lines. The act's line follows survey lines (the sixth and seventh standard parallels south of the Mount Diablo meridian) and takes in part of Buena Vista County, never organized and then part of Tulare: that part is not drawn. Congress never acted; the outline dates it to 1859, so the end is known to the year, drawn dashed. Not yet reviewed by the owner.

name: Territory of Jefferson
label: Jefferson Territory
source: Resolution of the Auraria convention, 15 April 1859, printed in the Cherry Creek Pioneer, 23 April 1859: from the 43rd parallel at the 102nd meridian west to the 110th, south to the 37th parallel, east to the 102nd; the organic act ratified on 24 October 1859 kept those bounds (J. C. Smiley, Semi-centennial History of the State of Colorado, 1913); Colorado Territory from 28 February 1861 (the Newberry)
note: The convention's text reckons the meridians "from Washington city"; every later text, and this map, reads them from Greenwich. The organic act's own text was not found: its bounds rest on Smiley. Not yet reviewed by the owner.

name: Sylvania
label: Sylvania
source: Report of the committee on a plan for the temporary government of the western territory, 1 March 1784 (the Avalon Project, Yale Law School): states two degrees of latitude apart, divided by the meridians of the lowest point of the rapids of the Ohio and of the western cape of the mouth of the Great Kanhaway, the land east of that meridian one state; and the ten names (Statehood Campaigns outline, Appendix A)
note: North of the 45th parallel, with the land north of the 47th that the report joins to it. The meridians pass through Wikidata's points for the Falls of the Ohio National Wildlife Conservation Area (Q3064799) and Tu-Endie-Wei State Park at the Kanawha's mouth (Q14714352): the report gives no degrees. Drawn on the federal territory the Newberry dates from Virginia's cession, 1 March 1784; the Ordinance of 23 April 1784 kept the lines and dropped the names. Not yet reviewed by the owner.

name: Confederate Territory of Arizona
label: Arizona (Confederate)
source: Baylor's proclamation at Mesilla, 1 August 1861: "all that portion of New Mexico lying south of the thirty-fourth parallel of north latitude" (Official Records, Series I, vol. 4, p. 20); the Confederate act of 18 January 1862 drew the same line (Statehood Campaigns outline, Appendix A)
note: The Confederates withdrew to Texas by July 1862 (the outline): the end is known to the month, drawn dashed. Not yet reviewed by the owner.

name: State of Lincoln
label: Lincoln
source: Handbook of Texas, "Division of Texas" (Claude Elliott): an 1869 proposal in Congress to divide Texas along the Colorado River, "the part south and west to be designated the state of Lincoln"; it never left committee (Statehood Campaigns outline, Appendix A)
note: Cut at Natural Earth's Colorado River of Texas, as the Nueces cut was made (the owner, 2026-11-18). The source does not say where the line runs beyond the river's head. Known to the year only: drawn dashed. Not yet reviewed by the owner.

name: State of Jefferson (1941)
label: Jefferson
source: The five county governments that endorsed it: Curry in Oregon; Siskiyou, Del Norte, Trinity and Modoc in California (the Oregon Encyclopedia, Jeff LaLande, "State of Jefferson"); its proclamation of 27 November 1941 (Jefferson Public Radio; Statehood Campaigns outline, Appendix A)
note: Gilbert Gable's plan of October 1941 named seven counties (Curry, Josephine, Jackson and Klamath in Oregon; Del Norte, Siskiyou and Modoc in California: this rests on Wikipedia alone), and Jackson and Josephine declined. Lassen County pledged on 27 November and is said to have withdrawn in December: not drawn. Pearl Harbor ended it: the end is known to the month, drawn dashed. Not yet reviewed by the owner.

name: Greater Idaho
label: Greater Idaho
kind: Counties that voted to join Idaho
source: Greater Idaho countywide ballot measures, 2020–2024 (Ballotpedia); OPB, 17 May and 9 November 2022; JPR, 19 May 2021; The Oregonian, 20 May 2026 (Wallowa's repeal)
